For example, visiting http://www.voat.co/ should log you out of your account. Removing the leading www. from the URL will log you back in. This also works if you log into your account while on a www. link and log out on a non-www. link. I can't test it since I don't have two accounts, but you can probably log into one account on http://voat.co/ and into another on http://www.voat.co/ and switch between them by adding or removing the www. in the URL. I feel like this could cause some confusion in the future if it stays like this, but it is kind of cool.

EDIT: Checking the cookies that are sent, the cfuid stays the same but the RequestVerificationToken changes when switching between www. links. They stay the same for their respective URLs, though.
Adding or removing www. in the URL allows you to switch accounts.

I think this sub is an awesome idea, and I really hope it can flourish, both for helping Voat out and to further my and other's own experience. With that in mind, we should have some sort of wiki or sticky or getting started guide. The voat source code has a README with some basic info on getting it installed (although I have no clue if/how it can be set up on my linux desktop, given that it's written in C# ASP.NET...) but that's about it.

I propose a TL;DR of sorts for the source code: a basic high-level overview describing it's architecture, which folders hold what important files, and which classes they should look at for a specific task. The overarching goal is that a new bug hunter should be able to read through it in less than 15 minutes and get an idea of where they should start looking. In addition to a few paragraphs describing the architecture and a section describing what each folder in the source code holds, we could have a list of popular actions (a user saves a comment, a user posts a link, a mod bans a user, etc.) and for each action, have a "stack trace" - what classes are doing what, and what other interactions they may trigger, and so on. The idea is that for example if someone is hunting a bug that occurs when a comment is saved, they should be able to look and see what class(es) are the best starting points to look at without having to parse through huge chunks of the source code just to get their bearings. The lower the barrier of entry for new hunters, the better!

TL;DR we need a wiki describing where to get started when reading through the voat source code.

I have never restarted a book that I gave up on, but I have a few that maybe I was too hasty to drop. I'm currently feeling tempted to try one or two again and I'm looking for some encouraging examples.
What book did you give up on, and then years later try again only to end up loving it?

Generally, it has mainly happened when the language, or subject matter is a little "out of my comfort zone"/"not quite what I am looking for at the moment". The one that comes to mind is David Foster Wallace's Infinite Jest. Definitely required reading, and loved it when I gave the book my proper attention. And I will be honest, I know it is more about me wanting to read a low-level trash pulp novel that fits more with escapism, and Infinite Jest didn't suite my mood when I first attempted it. EDITED: I have a soft spot for pulp stories, didn't feel right labeling it as trash.

Funny you should mention IJ- I came here with the intention of saying the same thing. It took me at least three good attempts before I finished that son of a bitch, and now it's one of my favorite books ever.
I just picked up his book, Oblivion: Stories. It looks like it is a much quicker read (gotta love short stories).

The Glass Bead Game by Hermann Hesse.

I went on a bit of a Hesse binge decades ago, and read Demian, Steppenwolf and Siddharta, but I just couldn't manage to make it through The Glass Bead Game.

Years later, I had a neighbor who said it was his favorite novel of all time, so I gave it another shot. I wouldn't rate it my favorite (in fact, it's not even my favorite Hesse), but it was well worth it.

Another one that's sort of notable for this is Thomas Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow, but that's a bit different. My opinion of it never really changed - I liked it even the first time I tried, and failed, to complete it. I didn't give up on it because I didn't like it, but just because it was so exhausting to read. I had to build up the initiative to make it all the way through it before I succeeded.

I'm digging through Hesse right now (loving it) and Gravity's Rainbow is on the shelf waiting patiently... I'm making up for all the fiction I missed while reading mountains of technical manuals the last 20 years...
If I can recommend this website for GR. As a younger reader it helped me with a lot of Pynchon's more obscure references.

I appreciate the thought, but I had no problem with Pynchon's references. It's not that it was that difficult to read in that sense. As I said, I found it exhausting. It was just the whole process of plowing through enormously long multi-layered sentences that are generally a veritable flood of metaphors.

Few writers could manage the complex sentences that Pynchon successfully used, or the marvelous metaphors that he came up with. So it would already be a bit of a challenge to read and appreciate him - comparable at least to Joyce or Melville. And Gravity's Rainbow is an extraordinarily dense wall of those complex sentences and marvelous metaphors - a deluge of them. That's why I read it, and why I enjoyed it, but also why it exhausted me, to the point that it took three tries before I made it all the way through it.

It's like... like listening to a virtuoso symphony orchestra playing free-form jazz. It's not just something one can sort of vaguely enjoy - to fully appreciate it requires a notable investment of energy and attention. And it just took a while before I was fully prepared to make that investment.

At first I was going to say Infinite Jest because, I mean, come on. That thing is a beast... but I think I'll say Blood Meridian by Cormac McCarthy. Something about the fever-dream narration and the intensely macabre nature of the content really baffled me. I just couldn't get into it in high school. I finally came back to it a few years ago and now it's one of my favorite American novels.

Here's my favorite passage- a single sentence with more poetic gravity than many other novels, even ambitious ones, manage to achieve in their entirety:

“A legion of horribles, hundreds in number, half naked or clad in costumes attic or biblical or wardrobed out of a fevered dream with the skins of animals and silk finery and pieces of uniform still tracked with the blood of prior owners, coats of slain dragoons, frogged and braided cavalry jackets, one in a stovepipe hat and one with an umbrella and one in white stockings and a bloodstained wedding veil and some in headgear or cranefeathers or rawhide helmets that bore the horns of bull or buffalo and one in a pigeontailed coat worn backwards and otherwise naked and one in the armor of a Spanish conquistador, the breastplate and pauldrons deeply dented with old blows of mace or sabre done in another country by men whose very bones were dust and many with their braids spliced up with the hair of other beasts until they trailed upon the ground and their horses' ears and tails worked with bits of brightly colored cloth and one whose horse's whole head was painted crimson red and all the horsemen's faces gaudy and grotesque with daubings like a company of mounted clowns, death hilarious, all howling in a barbarous tongue and riding down upon them like a horde from a hell more horrible yet than the brimstone land of Christian reckoning, screeching and yammering and clothed in smoke like those vaporous beings in regions beyond right knowing where the eye wanders and the lip jerks and drools.”

The Catcher In The Rye for me. It was required reading in school and I thought Holden was just an insufferable twat. After reading/hearing so many different opinions I picked it back up and read it all in a night. Then I waited a week or two and read it again.

Once I really started to analyze it, I could see why there was such appeal behind it. Don't get me wrong; I still feel Holden is an insufferable twat. But he's one I can connect to, at least a little bit.

Maybe I should give it yet another then. I really couldn't get past my complete and utter dislike of the main character. Yes, I understand that I hate him because of the skill of the author but I always found myself getting really annoyed.

Holden is a really interesting literary character. It seems most folks either completely empathize with him or absolutely abhor him. I started out despising him; he just seems like a whiny, entitled brat with no self-awareness. I wouldn't say that he grew on me, but after reading it multiple times I feel like I have at least some connection to him (I mean, don't we all go through times where we become disillusioned with someone/thing?).
Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is the one that comes to mind for me. I had a lot going on when I started it and ended up just giving up. Later I tried again and loved it.

The spiderwick chronicles. In grade 2, someone showed them to me, and I never read them because I didn't like spiders. Around grade 6, I decideed to read them anyways for some reason, and I've loved those books to this day.

The Hobbit and Lord of the Rings. I was assigned to read The Hobbit in school, therefore... hated it. When the movies of LOTR came out, i was put off by my hatred of The Hobbit and never watched them or read the books.

Then... i was bored one day two years ago and read LOTR. Now I LOVE IT! haha :)

My dad's friend gave me The Fellowship of the Ring in 1989 when I was 13. I tried to read it every time I found it but just couldn't get into it too all. Eventually I saw the film and thought that I'd better get to work on the books. I ended up ploughing through the three of them one after another and thoroughly enjoyed them all. I really can't face rereading them though.

Cloud Atlas by David Mitchell. The language and writing style at the beginning was "awful" and "incredibly boring". I stopped reading it and left it on the bedside table for years.

Then the movie was announced and the Wachowski's were directing. Ugh! Fine! I'll re-read it from the beginning and just power through. By the time I got to the end and (spoiler) the original language and writing style returned, I could not stop eating that sh*t up!

American Gods. I gave up after the first three chapters because the thing was reading as terrible self insert fan fiction. I couldn't believe people calling the main character "Shadow" in all seriousness.

I thought the author's (I wasn't familiar with Gaimen or his work at the time) thought process was something like this: Yeah, my protagonist is a super buff dude who wears all black and all the ladies want to do the sex with him and his name is Niel....I mean...Shadow.

A few years later I needed something to read and found the paper back (a friend had given it to me a long time ago). After getting through those first chapters the story immediately took off and it was a great and imaginative adventure.

It took me nearly 10 years to get through The Tin Drum... it starts off veeery slow. Also, I do not think I was ready to read it when I started.

There's several I have going right now that I keep putting down but they are not fiction... Goedel, Escher, Bach is turning into another multi-year read for me.

I am trying to read In Search of Lost Time in french, but I don't expect to get that one done until I am very old...
Something Happened by Joseph Heller. Can't say I loved it, but I felt accomplished for finishing it. I am probably one of the dozen or so people that can say they read the whole thing.

Atlas Shrugged. One of the longest books I have ever read. I read War and Peace right after that because I figured it took me a month to read Atlas Shrugged, why not another month on that? I didn't enjoy it as much. A Russian Downton Abby in my opinion.

Gardens of the Moon, Book 1 of the Malazan Book of the Fallen.

I fancied myself a 'sophisticated' fantasy novel connoisseur so I picked this up after seeing it in a bunch of lists. I must have tried 4 or 5 times to get into it. But I just couldn't do it. I thought I was used to authors that dropped you into their world without explaining things. I thought I liked that. Exposition is weakness! Characters don't explain the workings of the world to each other! They already know!

Holy shit that book was a slog. But by the end of the first one, I was aching to read the next. Then I was pissed that the story shifted to a different group for a while in the later books. And when Karsa came along, I wondered: who the hell cares about this dude? It was me. I cared. God dammit.

The first six boos are a slog ain't it? But personally I really loved book five for the wit and comic relief that is bugg and tehol. I couldn't believe that he was still introducing new characters up to the end... but damnit that man can build a world. Amazing writing and imagination.

I want to preface this by saying that Stephen King is one of the more difficult authors for me to sit down and read. I can read Chaucer and Shakespeare without issue, but King is so detail oriented that I cannot sit and read his books.

I received Bag of Bones as a birthday present and could NOT get past a certain point. I wanted to know what was going to happen, but I couldn't find the attention span to do it. So I broke down and cheated. I got the audio book. And holy crackers!!!!!

Gardens of the Moon it took me three readings since I bought it before I ever finished it recently. Somehow it now clicks with me and I am working through the series. I have read the Hobbit, LOTR, The Black Company with no problems but Gardens of the Moon was a show stopper for years.Loving it now. Matbe I had to be ready for it, since that seems to happen time to time with me on other books.

Gone with the Wind. I tried it when I was in middle school and thought it was the wordiest piece of crap ever written. Reading (or rather, listening to the audiobook) now and LOVE it. You don't realize just how complex of a character Scarlett is, and as well done as the movie is, a lot of it just doesn't do the book justice.

Arizona drug-tested 87,000 welfare recipients and found they are flushing taxpayer dollars

At the market one day and saw a woman with 5 gallons of apple juice 1 jar of yeast 5 pounds brown sugar 5 pounds white sugar and paid with what i learned was a EBT card( food stamps). What might you ask would she do with that, make apple wine. You see, you can't buy wine with EBT so she makes her own

Firstly I think that no state should be able to force people to take a drug test just because they are on welfare, except maybe (and I mean maybe, that really need a lot more debate) if there are strong suspicions that someone is addicted to some drug. If you do test people for drug you should help them when they test positive. Not reduce their opportunities in life even further by just cutting their benefits.

I see welfare just like work. If I can be drug tested to keep my job, they can be drug tested to keep benefits. Why should workers be held to a standard that people living off the system aren't subject to? I consider welfare a form of salary, your job on welfare is to be out looking for gainful employment and be drugfree.

Not such a bad comparison. But then I'm also very much opposed to drug testing of employees just because they are employees. I think that's a gross violation of someones privacy. There are some exception possible, maybe for jobs that require the utmost attention, jobs where you might put others in danger if you're under influence. But even then someone should be free to do something stupid on their time off without possibly risking his/her job. Why should a company be allowed (or asked) to take over the role of law-enforcement?
I can absolutely agree with that so long as they are clean or capable while on the job.

Indeed. A company has absolutely no business with what you do in your free time if it doesn't affect your work. Even if you decide to break the law in your weekends off, that's your choice (and for law enforcement to tackle of course).

Agreed. Advocates of welfare drug testing just want a fair system. Either eliminate the workplace drug testing requirement or also require it for welfare. Either one works for me. Just be consistent and fair

I do like that this article at least addresses the question (however briefly) of how many people either didn't apply for welfare due to the requirement or then refused to test: "More significantly, roughly 2,000 — one-third of applicants — failed to take the test." This has always been my main question in most news stories touting that it didn't save any money at all. I'm not necessarily in favor of the test being used to determine whether or not someone receives benefits (Think of the children!), but I do think it could lead to mandatory addiction counseling and possibly a way to ensure the benefits were actually being spent for the necessities of life and not more drugs.

Of course this only works in the case of mandatory testing for all users and not the way it was implemented in Arizona. "Do you do drugs? Yes/No If you answer yes, we're going to test you!"
